summary: Help learners (age 10–11) compare and order fractions, including fractions greater than 1, by reasoning about value rather than digit size. Core strategies: common denominators (always reliable), benchmarking to 1/2 and 1, and complement-to-1 for sets clustered just below a whole (e.g. 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12, where the gaps to 1 are 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12, so the smallest gap means the largest fraction). For fractions above 1, convert to a common denominator (7/5 = 21/15 vs 4/3 = 20/15) or to mixed numbers and place on a number line. Throughout, the discriminating goal is a justified ordering, since whole-number bias can produce a correct rank for the wrong reason on favourable sets.
misconceptions: Whole-number bias: bigger numerator and/or denominator means a bigger fraction (may land the right order for the wrong reason)
Compares numerators and denominators separately ('7 > 4 and 5 > 3 so 7/5 > 4/3')
Same-numerator lock reversed — with equal numerators, picks the bigger denominator as bigger (2/5 > 2/3)
Treats a fraction greater than 1 as if it were less than 1, or places it wrongly on the line
Compares without finding a common denominator

activities.title: Place and order fractions on a number line, measuring each gap to 1
steps: Place the set 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, 11/12 onto a number line running from 0 past 2.
For each fraction, mark or measure the distance from the fraction to the '1' mark (its gap to a whole): 3/4 → 1/4, 7/8 → 1/8, 5/6 → 1/6, 11/12 → 1/12.
State the order smallest to largest (3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12) and explain the link: the BIGGEST gap to 1 means the SMALLEST fraction, so 3/4 is smallest and 11/12 (hugging 1) is largest.
Place 7/5 and 4/3 on the same line and notice both land PAST 1; convert each to a mixed number (7/5 = 1 2/5) to confirm position.
Rewrite 7/5 and 4/3 over a common denominator (21/15 vs 20/15) and compare the numerators to decide which is larger.
Compare the counter-pair 2/3 and 2/5: which is larger, and why does the same number of larger-denominator pieces come to less?
activities.insight: Fraction size is one quantity located on the number line, not two independent whole numbers. For a near-whole set the fraction closest to 1 is largest; fractions greater than 1 sit past 1; and a common denominator turns any comparison into a single numerator comparison.

activities.title: Justify the ordering, not just the rank
steps: Order a fresh near-whole set (e.g. 2/3, 5/6, 9/10, 7/8) using the complement-to-1 method, writing each gap to 1 and explaining your reasoning.

Then tackle a pair where digit size and value DISAGREE — for example 5/6 vs 7/9, where '7 > 5 and 9 > 6' wrongly suggests 7/9 is larger — and settle it by writing both over a common denominator and comparing the deciding numerators.
Explain in words why comparing numerators and denominators separately is not a valid method, using the pair above as the case where it breaks down.
State for each answer the strategy you chose (common denominator, benchmark, or complement-to-1) and why it fitted those numbers.
activities.insight: A correct ranking is not the same as a correct method; the justification is what shows genuine understanding, and the chosen strategy should fit the numbers.

activities.title: Short comparison and placement checks
steps: Decide which is larger, 7/5 or 4/3, and show the common-denominator working.
Decide which is larger, 2/3 or 2/5, and explain the role of the denominator.
activities.insight: Learners can apply comparison strategies quickly and avoid common distractors (choosing 'equal', choosing 4/3 'because 4 and 3 are bigger', or choosing 2/5 because its denominator is larger).

activities.title: Reference fraction wall (support tool)
steps: Use a fraction wall extended past 1 to reveal which of two bars is longer and by how much.
Use it to check an ordering you have already reasoned out, or to settle a disputed pair.
activities.insight: A length model reinforces that fractions represent magnitudes that can be directly compared, including beyond one whole.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6 and 11/12 from smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided. Then compare 7/5 and 4/3 — which is larger?' Watch the strategy and listen to the justification.
checkAnswer: Smallest to largest: 3/4 < 5/6 < 7/8 < 11/12 (gaps to 1 are 1/4 > 1/6 > 1/8 > 1/12, so 3/4 is furthest below 1 and 11/12 closest). 7/5 > 4/3 (common denominator /15: 21/15 > 20/15).
